nodes.ask: A febrile infant or child in the ED. First moves?
options: Airway, breathing, circulation, consciousness; then vitals, weight and age in days
An antipyretic first, then judge how ill the child looks once the fever falls
Blood count, CRP, urine and a chest film first, before the child is examined
The height of the temperature first, since it separates serious infection from a virus
nodes.chainStep: Check the airway, breathing, circulation and consciousness; record temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, capillary refill and oxygen saturation (blood pressure if the pulse or refill is abnormal); weigh the child; note the age in days, gestation, vaccines, any rash and any seizure; think 'could this be sepsis?'
nodes.why: Immediately life-threatening features come first: the airway, breathing, circulation and the level of consciousness. Temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and capillary refill are measured in every febrile child, a weight is needed for every dose, and in a young infant the age in days and the appearance set the workup. A fall, or no fall, in temperature after an antipyretic does not separate serious from non-serious illness; after 6 months the height of the fever alone does not identify serious illness; and a child with no features of serious illness does not need routine blood tests or a chest film.

orders.dose: Temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and capillary refill time in every febrile child; blood pressure if the heart rate or capillary refill is abnormal

Pale, mottled, ashen or blue; no response to social cues; appears ill; does not wake or stay awake; weak, high-pitched or continuous cry; grunting; respiratory rate over 60; moderate or severe chest indrawing; reduced skin turgor; bulging fontanelle
A temperature of 38 C or higher puts the infant in the high-risk group; some vaccines cause fever at this age
Over 160 a minute under 12 months, over 150 at 12 to 24 months, over 140 at 2 to 5 years: at least intermediate risk
NICE: an electronic thermometer in the axilla under 4 weeks; axillary or infrared tympanic from 4 weeks to 5 years; oral and rectal routes not used routinely under 5
orders.note: AAP 2021 enrols infants with a documented rectal temperature of 38.0 C (100.4 F) or more, at home in the past 24 hours or in a clinical setting; NICE NG143 advises against routine rectal measurement under 5.

orders.dose: Taken seriously: infants febrile only at home had the same invasive bacterial infection rate (2.4%) as those febrile at assessment
Do not rely on a fall, or no fall, in temperature to separate serious from non-serious illness

nodes.note: Not in this version: children with a chronic illness or immune deficiency, returning travellers, newborns still in the nursery or neonatal unit, bronchiolitis and croup (the child who cannot breathe), and children over 5 beyond the shock, seizure, Kawasaki and MIS-C routes. Adult sepsis and meningitis are in pw_sepsis_fever; rashes in pw_rash; seizures in adults in pw_seizure.

nodes.label: Perfusion, convulsions, the skin and the first look

outcomes.if: Shocked, not convulsing; poor perfusion, mottled skin, slow capillary refill or low pressure

orders.dose: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg, may repeat once) or IV diazepam 0.15 to 0.2 mg/kg (maximum 10 mg, may repeat once); IM midazolam in the next order

orders.note: AES doses IM midazolam by weight band and gives no dose under 13 kg; JACEP Open doses it per kg: at 14 kg, 5 mg against 1.4 to 2.8 mg.

orders.dose: 2 mL/kg of 25% dextrose IV from 2 years; 4 mL/kg of 12.5% dextrose under 2 years

outcomes.if: Seizure over, 6 months to 5 years, waking; not shocked, no non-blanching rash
Seizure over, not a febrile seizure picture; under 6 months, over 5 years, or not waking

orders.dose: Immediate parenteral antibiotics if the child is unrousable; consider them with reduced consciousness, and look for meningitis and herpes simplex encephalitis
Suspect it with focal neurological signs, focal seizures or a decreased level of consciousness; give IV aciclovir
20 mg/kg over 1 hour every 8 hours for 10 days (US label, herpes simplex encephalitis); under 3 months: the newborn dose on the HSV route
A third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime or ceftriaxone until the cultures return; under 3 months add ampicillin or amoxicillin

Parenteral benzylpenicillin or a third-generation cephalosporin at the earliest opportunity

nodes.summary: Convulsing child: time the seizure and treat it from 5 minutes as status epilepticus. pw_seizure is for adults only, so the child's AES doses are here: IM midazolam 5 mg at 13 to 40 kg (10 mg over 40 kg; JACEP Open doses it at 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg), IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg) or IV diazepam 0.15 to 0.2 mg/kg (maximum 10 mg), and for a glucose under 60 mg/dL, 2 mL/kg of 25% dextrose from 2 years or 4 mL/kg of 12.5% dextrose under 2. Once it stops, a child of 6 months to 5 years who wakes returns to this pathway's febrile seizure route. Febrile status epilepticus carries the highest meningitis risk, and two guidelines advise an LP in every case.

A seizure with fever outside the febrile seizure picture (under 6 months, over 5 years, or a child who does not wake): look for bacterial meningitis, which NICE considers with a decreased level of consciousness or convulsive status epilepticus, and herpes simplex encephalitis, considered with focal signs, focal seizures or a decreased level of consciousness. Parenteral antibiotics go in immediately if the child is unrousable and are considered with any reduced consciousness; IV aciclovir is given when encephalitis is suggested. An infant under 3 months is worked up as a febrile young infant, a seizure being an HSV warning sign. pw_seizure and pw_ams are for adults only; the convulsing route here carries the AES weight-based doses.

Fever with a non-blanching rash: consider meningococcal disease, above all in an ill-looking child, with lesions over 2 mm, a capillary refill of 3 seconds or more, or neck stiffness, and give parenteral antibiotics at the earliest opportunity (benzylpenicillin or a third-generation cephalosporin, with ampicillin or amoxicillin added under 3 months). The rash and skin emergencies pathway (pw_rash) takes the purpura route from here, with its count, film, clotting and meningococcal workup; a child who becomes shocked comes back to this pathway's shock route.

nodes.ask: Fever and shock in a child. First hour?
options: Oxygen, IV or IO access, crystalloid boluses reassessed after each, antibiotics within 1 hour
Oxygen, IV or IO access, an LP with the blood culture, antibiotics once the CSF is in hand
Oxygen, IV or IO access, albumin boluses instead of crystalloid, antibiotics within 1 hour
Oxygen, IV or IO access, maintenance fluid only, antibiotics once a blood culture turns positive
nodes.chainStep: High-flow oxygen; IV or intraosseous access; blood culture, a gas with glucose and lactate, blood count, CRP, electrolytes, creatinine, liver tests and clotting; crystalloid bolus over minutes, reassessed after each; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour (ampicillin or amoxicillin added under 3 months); epinephrine or norepinephrine if shock persists; consultant and intensive care review; the LP only once stable
nodes.why: A child in septic shock gets antibiotics as soon as possible and ideally within 1 hour, after a blood culture that does not substantially delay them. Fluid goes in as crystalloid boluses, with the circulation reassessed after every one and the boluses stopped if shock resolves or fluid overload appears; SSC suggests crystalloid rather than albumin. A lumbar puncture waits until shock is treated, and antibiotics never wait for it. Withholding boluses is SSC's advice for sepsis without hypotension where there is no intensive care, not for a shocked child in an ED with intensive care behind it.

orders.dose: NICE: 10 mL/kg over under 10 minutes, at most 250 mL a bolus (10 to 20 mL/kg in newborns under 28 days), reassessed after each; SSC 2026: 10 to 20 mL/kg a bolus, up to 40 to 60 mL/kg in the first hour where intensive care is available
orders.note: NICE NG254 (1.9.1, 1.9.2) and NG143 (1.5.16) give 10 mL/kg a bolus; SSC 2026 (recommendation 19) allows 10 to 20 mL/kg a bolus up to 40 to 60 mL/kg in the first hour. Both reassess after every bolus.

orders.dose: SSC 2026: balanced or buffered crystalloid rather than 0.9% saline; NICE NG143: normally 0.9% sodium chloride; NICE NG254: glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 130 to 154 mmol/L
orders.note: SSC 2026 (recommendation 24) prefers balanced crystalloid; NICE NG143 1.5.16 starts with 0.9% saline; NG254 1.9.2 allows any glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 130 to 154 mmol/L.

orders.dose: Crystalloid rather than albumin for initial resuscitation
Septic shock: as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour; probable sepsis without shock: within 3 hours after rapid investigation (SSC); NICE: within 1 hour of meeting any high-risk criterion
Before antibiotics, when that does not substantially delay them
Measured as part of the first evaluation

NICE NG254: 80 mg/kg once a day (maximum 4 g) for suspected sepsis; US label: 50 to 75 mg/kg a day in 2 doses (maximum 2 g a day) for serious infections other than meningitis, 100 mg/kg (maximum 4 g) for meningitis; AAP 2021 (29 to 60 days): 50 mg/kg every 24 hours
orders.note: NICE gives 80 mg/kg once daily; the US label gives 50 to 75 mg/kg a day divided every 12 hours, or 100 mg/kg a day for meningitis; the AAP table gives 50 mg/kg every 24 hours for a well infant of 29 to 60 days.

orders.item: Ceftriaxone in a newborn under 28 days
orders.dose: NICE: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily for community-acquired sepsis if over 40 weeks corrected gestational age and not on an IV calcium infusion, otherwise cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 6 to 12 hours; the US label contraindicates ceftriaxone in premature neonates up to 41 weeks postmenstrual age, in hyperbilirubinemic neonates, and in neonates of 28 days or younger who need calcium-containing IV fluids

orders.dose: NICE: add ampicillin or amoxicillin to the cephalosporin for every infant under 3 months; AAP 2021: ampicillin in the 8 to 21 day regimens and for meningitis up to 28 days, ceftriaxone alone from 22 days for a UTI or no focus, with ampicillin added when listeria or enterococci are suspected
orders.note: Cephalosporins do not cover listeria (AAP KAS 5; StatPearls); the AAP calls listeria rare and adds ampicillin only when it is suspected after 21 days, while NICE NG143 1.5.7 and NG254 1.8.7 add it for every infant under 3 months.

orders.dose: Not until shock is treated and the child stabilised
For signs of shock or SpO2 under 92% in air
Reassess after each bolus; no improvement after a second bolus: a consultant attends in person
Epinephrine or norepinephrine, either first line; start through a peripheral vein rather than wait for central access
Infusion doses are not stated in the sources read
Not when stability returns with fluid and vasoactive drugs; SSC makes no recommendation either way for shock that stays unstable
Stress-dose corticosteroids for suspected or documented adrenal insufficiency

nodes.summary: Septic shock in a child: antibiotics within the hour after a blood culture, crystalloid boluses reassessed after each (10 mL/kg a bolus in NICE; 10 to 20 mL/kg up to 40 to 60 mL/kg in the first hour in SSC), epinephrine or norepinephrine through a peripheral line if shock persists, and intensive care. Once stable, the age-based routes in this pathway set the rest of the workup; an infant 60 days or younger still needs blood, urine and CSF cultures, with the LP done once it is safe.

nodes.summary: Outside the AAP well-appearing group: the 2021 guideline excludes infants born before 37 weeks, infants under 2 weeks whose perinatal course was complicated by maternal fever, infection or antibiotics, a high suspicion of HSV (such as vesicles), a focal bacterial infection, bronchiolitis, immune compromise, a neonatal course complicated by surgery or infection, congenital or chromosomal abnormalities, technology-dependent infants, and immunization in the previous 48 hours; they are managed individually and are not covered in this version. NICE applies its under-3-months rules to every febrile infant: count, blood culture, CRP and urine; an LP and parenteral antibiotics under 1 month, when unwell, or with a white count under 5 or over 15. After vaccines: some vaccines cause fever under 3 months, and in one series all 35 infants seen within 72 hours of meningococcal B vaccine had vaccine fever without invasive infection; within 12 to 24 hours of that vaccine the review finds it reasonable to limit tests, withhold antibiotics and observe, with a urinalysis considered and the CRP often raised by the vaccine.

nodes.ask: Febrile at 7 days or younger, or ill-appearing at 8 to 60 days. Next?
options: Blood culture, catheter urine, LP, count and CRP; admit; parenteral antibiotics
Blood culture and urine; an LP only if the CRP or procalcitonin is raised
Blood culture, urine and an LP; parenteral antibiotics once a culture turns positive
Count and CRP first; cultures, LP and antibiotics only if either is raised
nodes.chainStep: Blood culture; catheter urine for urinalysis and culture (not routine in the first 72 hours after birth in NICE); LP for CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain and culture, with HSV PCR for any HSV feature; blood count and CRP (or procalcitonin); stool culture with diarrhea, chest film with respiratory signs; admit; parenteral antibiotics within 1 hour of the decision; if the infant is unstable the LP waits, the antibiotics do not
nodes.why: A febrile newborn in the first week, or any ill-appearing young infant, gets the full evaluation: blood culture, urine, cerebrospinal fluid, a blood count and CRP, then admission and parenteral antibiotics within an hour of the decision, without waiting for results. NICE does an LP and gives parenteral antibiotics to every febrile infant under 1 month and every unwell infant of 1 to 3 months, and the AAP 2021 guideline covers only well-appearing infants of 8 to 60 days. Letting the markers decide the LP is the route for well-appearing infants of 22 days and over.

Every febrile infant under 1 month; every unwell infant of 1 to 3 months; 1 to 3 months with a white count under 5 or over 15 x 10^9/L; without delay and, when possible, before antibiotics
Stabilise the airway, breathing, shock, seizures or bleeding risk first; no LP with extensive or spreading purpura, infection at the site or signs of raised pressure
Red and white cell counts with differential, protein, glucose with a blood glucose just before the LP, Gram stain, culture and PCR for relevant pathogens
As soon as possible and always within 1 hour of the decision to treat

nodes.ask: Febrile at 21 days or younger, or ill-appearing at 28 days or younger. Regimen?
options: IV ampicillin plus gentamicin, or ampicillin plus a third-generation cephalosporin
IV ceftriaxone given with calcium-containing IV fluids, since it also covers listeria
IV vancomycin plus gentamicin, keeping ampicillin for a positive culture
IV gentamicin alone, adding a cephalosporin only if the CSF is abnormal
nodes.chainStep: IV ampicillin 150 mg/kg a day divided every 8 hours with ceftazidime 150 mg/kg a day divided every 8 hours or gentamicin 4 mg/kg every 24 hours (AAP 2021, 8 to 21 days; the US labels dose ceftazidime and gentamicin lower in neonates); acyclovir for any HSV feature; first dose within 1 hour
nodes.why: Ampicillin is part of every regimen at this age because it covers group B streptococcus and listeria, and cephalosporins do not cover listeria or enterococci. For a well infant of 8 to 21 days the AAP gives ampicillin with ceftazidime or gentamicin; for newborns StatPearls gives ampicillin with an aminoglycoside or with a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime, ceftazidime or cefepime). Ceftriaxone does not cover listeria, and in a newborn of 28 days or younger it is contraindicated with calcium-containing IV fluids; vancomycin is for the infant with severe infection or instability; and gentamicin without ampicillin leaves group B streptococcus and listeria uncovered.

Manage constipation and voiding problems, and tell the parents that UTIs can recur and need prompt treatment.

A UTI not better at 48 hours, or atypical (seriously ill, poor urine flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, septicemia, a non-E. coli organism): an ultrasound during the acute infection for obstruction or an abscess, the culture and antibiotic reviewed, and parenteral treatment if the child cannot take oral medicine or is worsening. NICE adds a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months later under 3 years, an MCUG under 6 months, and considers one from 6 months to 3 years for dilatation, poor flow, a non-E. coli infection or a family history of reflux.

nodes.why: A fever of 5 days or longer calls for an assessment for Kawasaki disease: bilateral conjunctival injection without exudate, red cracked lips, a strawberry tongue or red mouth, red swollen hands and feet, a polymorphous rash and a cervical node over 1.5 cm, asked about since the fever began because they may have gone by the time of the visit. Infants under 1 year may show fewer features but carry a higher coronary risk. Fever over 24 hours with 2 or more organs involved and raised inflammatory markers after SARS-CoV-2 raises MIS-C. Waiting, or treating it as occult bacteremia, delays the echocardiogram and IVIG, and a late Kawasaki diagnosis can be catastrophic.

nodes.summary: Kawasaki disease: an echocardiogram at diagnosis, IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours with aspirin 80 to 100 mg/kg a day in 4 doses until afebrile for over 48 hours, then 3 to 5 mg/kg a day, ideally within 7 to 10 days of fever onset; a child still febrile 36 to 48 hours after IVIG gets a second dose. Incomplete Kawasaki follows the AHA laboratory and echocardiogram algorithm. pw_rash carries the Kawasaki flags too; the AHA statements themselves (ahajournals) were not read.

Possible MIS-C: fever over 24 hours, 2 or more organs involved, raised inflammatory markers and SARS-CoV-2 infection or contact. First-step bloods, troponin and NT-proBNP, an ECG and an echocardiogram; shock can be the first sign or come on quickly in hospital. The Italian guidance treats with IVIG 2 g/kg over at least 12 hours, glucocorticoids with it for heart involvement or severe disease, aspirin 5 mg/kg for at least 6 to 8 weeks, and broad-spectrum antibiotics while infection is excluded. Not covered further in this version.

Two or three features with a CRP under 30 mg/L and an ESR under 40 mm/hr: review daily, with an echocardiogram if the fever settles and the skin peels; an infant under 6 months with over 7 days of fever gets an echocardiogram. Fever of 5 days or more without Kawasaki or MIS-C features: duration alone does not predict serious illness, so the source is sought as for any febrile child, and the Kawasaki features are asked about again, since they may have resolved by the time of assessment. Not covered further in this version.

Fever with a clear source in a child over 60 days: pneumonia goes to pw_peds_breathing and a septic hip to pw_hot_joint; otitis, osteomyelitis and skin infections are not covered in this version. NICE considers pneumonia with fast breathing, crackles, nasal flaring, chest indrawing, cyanosis or a saturation of 95% or less, and septic arthritis or osteomyelitis with a swollen limb or joint, an unused limb or no weight bearing. A fever lasting 5 days or more is still assessed for Kawasaki disease.

nodes.why: A febrile seizure is a seizure with a fever of at least 38 C, without CNS infection, at 6 to 60 months. The history (generalized or focal, how long, how many in 24 hours, back to baseline or not), the Hib and pneumococcal vaccine record, any antibiotics, and an examination for meningitis and the fever's source sort simple from complex seizures and pick out the child who needs an LP. A glucose is checked as for any seizure, but routine laboratory tests are not needed after a simple febrile seizure, the AAP advises against routine neuroimaging, and no EEG is done in a neurologically healthy child with a simple febrile seizure.

nodes.summary: Simple febrile seizure at 12 months or older, back to baseline with no meningism: no LP, EEG, neuroimaging or routine blood tests; find and treat the fever's source, and most children go home after a period of observation. Reassure the parents: about a third have another febrile seizure, 1% to 2% later develop epilepsy, and there is no lasting neurological harm. Antipyretics make the child comfortable but do not prevent seizures, and continuous or intermittent antiseizure prophylaxis is not advised. During a seizure: on the side on a safe surface, nothing in the mouth, time it, and call an ambulance if it lasts over 5 minutes.

Simple febrile seizure at 6 to 11 months, or in a child already on antibiotics: the AAP makes the LP an option at 6 to 12 months when Hib or pneumococcal vaccination is incomplete or unknown, and in a child pretreated with antibiotics, which can mask meningitis; the Italian review goes further and strongly recommends an LP under 1 year. A child who has an LP after a febrile seizure is admitted. Otherwise as for a simple febrile seizure: no EEG, imaging or routine bloods, and reassurance. A fully vaccinated infant of 6 to 11 months who is not on antibiotics meets neither AAP option, so no LP in the AAP approach; the Italian review still strongly recommends one under 1 year.

Fever, a seizure and meningitis signs: an LP when it is safe, parenteral antibiotics not delayed for it (a third-generation cephalosporin, with vancomycin over 1 month in IDSA 2004 but not in NICE), IV dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours with or before the first antibiotic for strongly suspected bacterial meningitis over 3 months of age (IDSA does not start it once antibiotics are in; NICE allows up to 12 hours), and aciclovir if focal seizures or signs suggest herpes simplex encephalitis; admit. NICE NG240 covers children with meningitis; the CSF route in pw_sepsis_fever is written for adults.

Complex febrile seizure without meningitis signs: no national guideline sets the workup, so it is individualized. An EEG, above all with an abnormal neurological or developmental status; neuroimaging if a postictal neurological deficit is present; an LP under 12 months in two guidelines, or only if the examination suggests meningitis in another; admission for observation in selected cases; neurology follow-up. Epilepsy follows in 4% to 15%, depending on the number of complex features.
